The post Oakland kids can now borrow sports gear for free at this special library first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Youth sports in the United States now cost the average family about $1,016 a year per child, up 46 percent since 2019, according to the Aspen Institute’s 2025 State of Play report. In Oakland, where just 14 percent of kids get the recommended 60 minutes of daily physical activity, compared to a national average of 23 percent, that number matters.

Maribel Lopez spent 18 years working for Oakland’s parks and recreation department watching that play out. When she had budget left at the end of the year, she decided to do something with it.

What the library actually is

The Park Play Lending Library opened July 11 at the Larry E. Reid Sports Center in Brookfield Village, just south of the Coliseum in East Oakland. The setup is exactly what it sounds like: check out a soccer ball or jump rope, take it to the park, bring it back. Footballs, volleyballs, yoga mats, and tennis equipment are in the rotation. People asked for board games, so those are in there now too.

“The library is just at the beginning stages right now,” said Riles Nganga, a recreation leader at the center. “Everything isn’t even here yet, so we still want to get spike ball out here. Anything that can get people outside, outdoors, moving and not being in the house sedentary.”

The neighborhood it was built for

Brookfield Village has fewer parks, less green space, and fewer city resources than most Oakland neighborhoods, but a lot of kids.

The sports center has been filling that kind of gap for a while. When it opened in 2011, it brought the first public pool to the neighborhood since 1976. For the three decades in between, families made do with a contaminated estuary nearby. “Kids were talking about being Olympic gold-medal swimmers but we had nowhere to learn,” community representative Jacquee Castain said in 2009, two years before the pool finally opened.

Maria Garcia works the front desk at the center and hears the same thing about equipment. “Parents are trying to keep food on the table, but also navigate being able to have their kids go to things and participate in things, and sometimes, it can be difficult,” she said. “And I think having resources like this kind of opens up that door for them to be able to do that.”

What sparked this ingenious idea?

Tool-lending libraries have been running in Oakland and Berkeley for years: you borrow a drill the same way you’d borrow a book, use it, bring it back. Lopez saw the same logic applying to a soccer ball.

She noticed families kept showing up at the center asking to borrow equipment, especially as summer approached. She held onto the idea until she had a little budget left and a reason to move on it.

Her case for why this matters goes beyond physical activity. “We’re aware that sports can lead to social mobility,” she told SFGATE. “When kids are familiar with golf, tennis, soccer, and other games or sports that are more socially mobile, then they have access to different communities, different friend groups, different neighborhoods, and we want to be a vehicle for that. We want kids to be able to speak each other’s language and connect through sports.”

Nganga, who grew up in Brookfield Village, didn’t need much convincing. “I know growing up, I didn’t have access to any of this stuff, so I think us being able to offer that to the community is a great thing.”

What happens next

This is a pilot. If it holds here, the plan is one lending library per Oakland district, each stocked based on what that community asks for. Partnerships with local sports organizations are in the works too.

The World Cup renewed a familiar conversation this year about cost being the wall between American kids and competitive youth sports. A lending library in East Oakland doesn’t knock that wall down. But the idea that a ball you can borrow is as useful as one you own is simple, cheap, and replicable, and it’s already in the hands of kids who didn’t have one before.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.title: Mountaineer who began fossil hunting after near-death experience discovers rare 'sea dragon'
articles.summary: Matthew Myerscough swapped mountains for fossil-laden beaches after becoming trapped in snow on Yr Wyddfa.
articles.content:
A mountaineer who nearly died in an avalanche has described how his recovery led him to amateur fossil hunting and the discovery of a marine reptile or "sea dragon" not found in Wales before.

Matthew Myerscough said he was left with post-traumatic stress disorder after being unconscious for 20 minutes buried beneath a metre of snow after a slide on Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, in 2014.

It led him away from the mountains to fossil-laden beaches at Lavernock Point in the Vale of Glamorgan, where he discovered a jaw bone from the Jurassic period 200 million years ago.

Myerscough, a civil engineer, said the painstaking process of fossil hunting helped his worries and stresses to "melt away".

"Looking back now, I realise, I have had some PTSD, external," he said of the accident.

Myerscough returned to Yr Wyddfa in 2018 for the Dragon's Back Challenge, hiking past the place where he had almost died, but said by then he was moving away from mountaineering.

"Being on the beach, and looking for fossils, and being kind of really focused on one specific task... it has been a tool for me to kind of process things," he said.

"Worries or stresses kind of melt away as you're focused," he said, comparing it to the mindfulness people can get from yoga, sport or watching a film.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful personal recovery journey where a near-death experience led to a positive mental health outcome through fossil hunting, culminating in the discovery of a rare marine reptile fossil. This story has broad inspirational value and highlights mental health benefits from nature-related activities, as well as a tangible scientific discovery with regional significance.
articles.personality_title: Mountaineer’s near-death experience leads to discovery of rare ancient sea reptile
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2014, Matthew Myerscough, a mountaineer, was caught in an avalanche on Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) and buried under snow for 20 minutes. This traumatic event caused him to develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

**What happened** – After his recovery, Myerscough shifted his focus from climbing mountains to searching for fossils on beaches at Lavernock Point in Wales. There, he found a rare jaw bone from a marine reptile, known as a 'sea dragon,' dating back 200 million years to the Jurassic period.

**Impact** – This discovery is significant because such fossils had not been found in Wales before. Additionally, the careful and focused activity of fossil hunting helped Myerscough manage his PTSD by giving him a calming and purposeful task, similar to mindfulness practices.

**What's next step** – Myerscough’s find may encourage more fossil hunting in the area, possibly leading to new discoveries about ancient marine life. His story also shows how nature activities can support mental health, which could inspire others facing similar challenges.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After surviving an avalanche, a mountaineer found healing through fossil hunting and uncovered a rare 200-million-year-old marine reptile fossil in Wales.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un alpiniste découvre un rare reptile marin ancien après une expérience proche de la mort
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2014, Matthew Myerscough, un alpiniste, a été pris dans une avalanche sur Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) et enseveli sous la neige pendant 20 minutes. Cet événement traumatisant lui a causé un trouble de stress post-traumatique (TSPT).

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Après sa guérison, Myerscough s’est tourné vers la recherche de fossiles sur les plages de Lavernock Point au Pays de Galles. Il y a trouvé une mâchoire rare d’un reptile marin, appelé « dragon de mer », datant de 200 millions d’années, à l’époque du Jurassique.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car de tels fossiles n’avaient jamais été trouvés auparavant au Pays de Galles. De plus, l’activité attentive de recherche de fossiles a aidé Myerscough à gérer son TSPT en lui offrant une tâche apaisante et pleine de sens, semblable à la pleine conscience.

**Prochaine étape** – Cette trouvaille pourrait encourager davantage de recherches de fossiles dans la région, menant à de nouvelles découvertes sur la vie marine ancienne. L’histoire de Myerscough montre aussi comment les activités en nature peuvent soutenir la santé mentale, ce qui pourrait inspirer d’autres personnes.

**En une phrase** – Après avoir survécu à une avalanche, un alpiniste a trouvé la guérison grâce à la recherche de fossiles et a découvert un rare fossile de reptile marin vieux de 200 millions d’années au Pays de Galles.
articles.personality_title_es: Montañero descubre raro reptil marino antiguo tras experiencia cercana a la muerte
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2014, Matthew Myerscough, un montañero, quedó atrapado en una avalancha en Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) y estuvo enterrado bajo la nieve durante 20 minutos. Este evento traumático le causó trastorno de estrés postraumático (TEPT).

**Qué pasó** – Después de su recuperación, Myerscough cambió su enfoque de escalar montañas a buscar fósiles en las playas de Lavernock Point en Gales. Allí encontró un hueso de mandíbula raro de un reptil marino, llamado «dragón marino», que data de hace 200 millones de años, del período Jurásico.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque esos fósiles no se habían encontrado antes en Gales. Además, la actividad cuidadosa y concentrada de buscar fósiles ayudó a Myerscough a manejar su TEPT al darle una tarea calmante y con propósito, parecida a la atención plena.

**Próximo paso** – El descubrimiento podría motivar más búsquedas de fósiles en la zona, llevando a nuevos hallazgos sobre la vida marina antigua. La historia de Myerscough también muestra cómo las actividades en la naturaleza pueden apoyar la salud mental y puede inspirar a otros.

**Una frase clave** – Tras sobrevivir a una avalancha, un montañero encontró sanación buscando fósiles y descubrió un raro fósil de reptil marino de 200 millones de años en Gales.
